title: Standardize autocapitalize, IME, and keyboard behaviors for international text inputs
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Problem: Input behavior across platforms is inconsistent for international users. Autocapitalize, IME composition handling, and keyboard types differ between iOS/Android/desktop and between browser vendors. This causes unexpected autocorrections, incorrect casing in identifiers (email/handles), and broken composition for languages using IMEs (Chinese, Japanese, Korean).

Goal: Define a single, pragmatic design and engineering spec for Redwood form components (TextField, Multiline, Email, Search, Password, Numeric) that standardizes attributes and platform fallbacks so developers get predictable behavior without per-field custom hacks. The spec should: 1) minimize accidental corrections for identifiers and codes; 2) preserve IME composition for CJK languages; 3) set sensible keyboardType/inputmode defaults; 4) document token/variant mappings so Console/SDK teams can apply consistent props; 5) include accessibility guidance for screen readers and announce composition state when appropriate.
acceptance_criteria: TextField default prop mapping defined: autocapitalize='off' for single-line token-like fields and 'sentences' for rich text areas
IME composition preserved for Multiline and single-line inputs when language tag or inputMode indicates CJK or other composition-heavy languages
Email and username fields set inputmode/email and autocorrect/off with clear guidelines to avoid capitalization and suggestions
Platform quirks table created (iOS Safari, Android Chrome, macOS Safari/Chrome, Windows Edge) with recommended fallbacks and rationale
Design tokens documented for label/microcopy states explaining why certain fields disable autocorrect or change keyboard hints
Console and SDK owners have a clear migration plan and a feature flag for staged rollout
Automated test plans enumerated for keyboard capture, composition commit, and mobile keyboard type assertions
tasks: Audit existing codebase for explicit input attributes (autocapitalize/autocorrect/inputmode/type) across components and app integrations
Create platform quirks matrix and sample repros for each problematic combination
Draft canonical prop table for each component variant with recommended defaults
Update design tokens doc and component API docs with examples and microcopy guidance
Implement changes in the component library behind a feature flag and add unit/e2e tests for composition behavior
Run a staged rollout with Console routes flagged and collect error/behavior telemetry
Ship migration guide and RFC for SDKs with changelog entries and sample code snippets
decisions: Default single-line text inputs that are meant for free text will use autocapitalize='sentences' unless field intent is clearly identifier-like (email, handle, code)
Identifier-like inputs (email, username, slug, promo code) default to autocapitalize='off' and autocorrect='off' to avoid accidental changes
Multiline inputs preserve IME composition by ensuring composition events are not suppressed and by avoiding programmatic value resets during composition
Inputmode (numeric, tel, email, search) will be advertised via inputmode/type props where supported; fallback heuristics documented for platforms that ignore inputmode
We will not attempt to detect locale from device for deciding autocapitalize — relying on explicit field intent and developer override to avoid privacy/edge cases
tradeoffs: Conservative defaults (off for autocorrect/autocapitalize) reduce accidental data changes but may hurt casual typing discoverability for non-technical users
Preserving IME composition everywhere prevents some eager formatting UX (eg. auto-trimming spaces) which teams must consider when validating input live
Relying on developer-provided field intent keeps API simple but may result in inconsistent integrations; mitigated via Console linting and SDK helpers
Platform-specific hacks (CSS/inputmode workarounds) increase maintenance cost; preferred to document and avoid unless necessary for accessibility/regulatory reasons
